s2.title: A sentence cut into tokens

s3.chapterTitle: Your question is chopped into tokens
s3.title: The context window fills up
s3.caption: Your question, the chat so far and the answer being written all share one fixed space. When it's full, something has to give: many apps drop or summarise the oldest messages.

s4.chapterTitle: Each word becomes a point in space
s4.title: Token numbers versus embeddings
s4.caption: A token number is just a label. An embedding is a pattern of numbers, and similar meanings get similar patterns. Values made up for this example.
s4.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 368" role="img" aria-labelledby="s4-illEmT s4-illEmD" width="100%">
    <title id="s4-illEmT">Token numbers versus embeddings</title>
    <desc id="s4-illEmD">Top: token numbers 9,412, 9,413 and 9,414 stand for sky, jumped and Paris. Next-door numbers, unrelated words. Bottom: each word's embedding is drawn as a strip of coloured cells. The strips for sky and cloud have almost the same pattern. The strip for sandwich looks quite different. Similar patterns mean similar meanings.</desc>
    <g font-family="'AIAD Sans',Arial,sans-serif" fill="#231F20" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32)">
      <text x="20" y="28" font-size="13" font-weight="800" letter-spacing=".08em" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:13px;font-weight:800;letter-spacing:1.04px">TOKEN NUMBERS</text>
      <rect x="20" y="44" width="72" height="26" fill="#ece8de" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1" style="fill:rgb(236, 232, 222);stroke:rgb(35, 31, 32)"></rect><text x="56" y="62" font-family="ui-monospace,Menlo,Consolas,monospace" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:15px;text-anchor:middle">9,412</text><text x="102" y="62" font-size="15" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:15px">→ “sky”</text><rect x="20" y="76" width="72" height="26" fill="#ece8de" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1" style="fill:rgb(236, 232, 222);stroke:rgb(35, 31, 32)"></rect><text x="56" y="94" font-family="ui-monospace,Menlo,Consolas,monospace" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:15px;text-anchor:middle">9,413</text><text x="102" y="94" font-size="15" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:15px">→ “jumped”</text><rect x="20" y="108" width="72" height="26" fill="#ece8de" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1" style="fill:rgb(236, 232, 222);stroke:rgb(35, 31, 32)"></rect><text x="56" y="126" font-family="ui-monospace,Menlo,Consolas,monospace" font-size="15" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:15px;text-anchor:middle">9,414</text><text x="102" y="126" font-size="15" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:15px">→ “Paris”</text>

s7.chapterTitle: The trip to a building full of chips
s7.title: Your question's journey to a data centre
s7.caption: Cloud AI: the model runs in a data centre, and you reach it over the internet. Running the already-trained model to answer you is inference.
s7.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 236" role="img" aria-labelledby="s7-illCdT s7-illCdD" width="100%">
    <title id="s7-illCdT">Your question's journey to a data centre</title>
    <desc id="s7-illCdD">Your phone sends the question as pulses of light along a fibre-optic cable, which may run under the sea, to a data centre full of racks of chips. Inference happens there: the trained model runs. The answer streams back along the same route, token by token.</desc>
    <g font-family="'AIAD Sans',Arial,sans-serif" fill="#231F20" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32)">
      <text x="220" y="24" font-size="15" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:15px;font-weight:700;text-anchor:middle">Question →  travels as light</text>

s8.chapterTitle: Thousands of workers, one huge sum
s8.title: Multiplying a matrix: many separate sums
s8.caption: A matrix multiplication is lots of small, separate sums, which is exactly the kind of work thousands of GPU cores can share. Real models use grids with thousands of rows and columns.
s8.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 252" role="img" aria-labelledby="s8-illMxT s8-illMxD" width="100%">
    <title id="s8-illMxT">Multiplying a matrix: many separate sums</title>
    <desc id="s8-illMxD">A four-by-four grid of the model's numbers is multiplied by a column of four numbers for one token. Each of the four results is its own sum of one row times the column, for example 2 times 1 plus 0 times 2 plus 1 times 0 plus 3 times 1 equals 5. No sum waits for another, so all four can be worked out at the same time.</desc>

s9.chapterTitle: Thousands of workers, one huge sum
s9.title: Quantisation: fewer bits, rounded numbers
s9.caption: 4 bits allow only 16 different values, so every number is rounded to the nearest one: a quarter of the memory, a little less precision. Simplified: real methods also store a scale for each group of numbers.

s10.chapterTitle: Printing with light no one can see
s10.title: Who builds an AI chip
s10.caption: Simplified: hundreds more companies supply tools, chemicals and parts. Each one builds on the others, so a problem with any single link, such as an export ban, can hold up the whole chain.
s10.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 724" role="img" aria-labelledby="s10-illScT s10-illScD" width="100%">
    <title id="s10-illScT">Who builds an AI chip</title>
    <desc id="s10-illScD">The supply chain for one AI chip. Design: NVIDIA in the USA designs it, using chip-design software from Synopsys and Cadence. Machines: ASML in the Netherlands builds the EUV machines, using mirrors from Zeiss and lasers from Trumpf in Germany. Materials: silicon wafers from Shin-Etsu and SUMCO in Japan, and gallium and germanium mostly from China. All three flow into making: TSMC in Taiwan prints the design onto wafers. Memory chips called HBM come from SK hynix and Samsung in South Korea and Micron in the USA. TSMC packages the chip and its memory together, giving an AI chip ready for a data centre. At least seven countries are involved, and none can do it alone.</desc>

s11.chapterTitle: The model guesses the next word, again and again
s11.title: Attention: "blue" looks back at the words before it
s11.caption: Each token gives every earlier token a score, then blends in information from the ones that score highest. It can't look ahead: the words after it haven't been written yet.
s11.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 330" role="img" aria-labelledby="s11-illAtT s11-illAtD" width="100%">
    <title id="s11-illAtT">Attention: "blue" looks back at the words before it</title>
    <desc id="s11-illAtD">The tokens Why, is, the, sky, blue and a question mark. Curved lines run from "blue" back to each earlier token. The line to "sky" is by far the thickest: blue gives sky 75 percent of its attention, the others 5 or 10 percent. The question mark comes later, so blue cannot look at it. After attention, "blue" no longer means a colour or a mood: it means the colour of the sky.</desc>

s12.chapterTitle: The model guesses the next word, again and again

s13.chapterTitle: Every model is built from other models' ideas
s13.title: Training: guess, check, nudge, repeat
s13.caption: Training adjusts the parameters a tiny bit after every guess. After training they're fixed: answering your question (inference) changes nothing. Percentages made up for this example.
s13.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 290" role="img" aria-labelledby="s13-illTrT s13-illTrD" width="100%">
    <title id="s13-illTrT" style="font-size:18.02px">Training: guess, check, nudge, repeat</title>
    <desc id="s13-illTrD" style="font-size:18.02px">The model reads "The sky is" from its training text, with the next word hidden. It guesses: blue 30 percent, green 25 percent, grey 15 percent. It checks the real next word, which is blue. Then its parameters are nudged so that blue scores a little higher next time, 30 percent becomes 33 percent. This repeats for every token, trillions of times, over months.</desc>

s14.chapterTitle: Every model is built from other models' ideas
s14.title: One model, many sources: DeepSeek-V3
s14.caption: DeepSeek-V3 mixes ideas from US and Chinese labs, and its own ideas were then picked up in both countries. Simplified: only some of its parts are shown. Source: Sebastian Raschka, "How LLMs build on each other" (llm-gallery.com).

s15.chapterTitle: Every model is built from other models' ideas
s15.title: Closed models and open-weight models
s15.caption: Open weights let anyone build on a model, which is how ideas spread between labs, including across borders. Most come with a licence that sets some rules.
s15.svg:

s16.chapterTitle: Every model is built from other models' ideas
s16.title: Distillation: a small student learns from a big teacher

s17.chapterTitle: The answer comes home, and you check it
s17.title: A hallucination looks just as sure as a fact
s17.caption: Fluent and confident isn't the same as correct. The only way to catch it was to check against a trusted source. (Blue taken as 450 nm, red as 700 nm.)
s17.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 330" role="img" aria-labelledby="s17-illHaT s17-illHaD" width="100%">
    <title id="s17-illHaT">A hallucination looks just as sure as a fact</title>
    <desc id="s17-illHaD">Two sentences from the chatbot's answer, written in exactly the same confident style. The first, shorter wavelengths scatter far more than longer ones, is right. The second, the effect depends on the wavelength to the power of two, is wrong. Your notes say intensity goes as one over wavelength to the power four, which shows the second sentence is a hallucination. It matters: with the right formula, blue light at 450 nanometres scatters about 6 times more than red at 700 nanometres. The wrong formula gives only about 2.4 times.</desc>
    <g font-family="'AIAD Sans',Arial,sans-serif" fill="#231F20" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32)">
      <text x="20" y="24" font-size="13" font-weight="800" letter-spacing=".08em" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:13px;font-weight:800;letter-spacing:1.04px">THE ANSWER ON YOUR SCREEN</text>
      <rect x="20" y="36" width="400" height="40" fill="#fff" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.5" style="fill:rgb(255, 255, 255);stroke:rgb(35, 31, 32);stroke-width:1.5px"></rect>
      <text x="32" y="61" font-size="14" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:14px">Shorter wavelengths scatter far more than longer ones.</text>
      <rect x="20" y="84" width="400" height="40" fill="#fde8e8" stroke="#d93025" stroke-width="2.5" style="fill:rgb(253, 232, 232);stroke:rgb(217, 48, 37);stroke-width:2.5px"></rect>
      <text x="32" y="109" font-size="14" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:14px">It depends on the wavelength to the power of two.</text>
      <rect x="20" y="140" width="190" height="62" fill="#FFF3C4" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.5" style="fill:rgb(255, 243, 196);stroke:rgb(35, 31, 32);stroke-width:1.5px"></rect>
      <text x="32" y="160" font-size="12" font-weight="800" letter-spacing=".06em" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:12px;font-weight:800;letter-spacing:0.72px">YOUR NOTES</text>
      <text x="32" y="188" font-family="Georgia,'Times New Roman',serif" font-size="18" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:18px">I ∝ 1/λ⁴</text>
      <path d="M216 171H262V134" fill="none" stroke="#d93025" stroke-width="2" style="fill:none;stroke:rgb(217, 48, 37);stroke-width:2px"></path><path d="M262 128l-5 10h10z" fill="#d93025" style="fill:rgb(217, 48, 37)"></path>
      <text x="274" y="160" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#9b1c14" style="fill:rgb(155, 28, 20);font-size:14px;font-weight:700">Checked: the</text>
      <text x="274" y="178" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#9b1c14" style="fill:rgb(155, 28, 20);font-size:14px;font-weight:700">second sentence</text>
      <text x="274" y="196" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#9b1c14" style="fill:rgb(155, 28, 20);font-size:14px;font-weight:700">is a hallucination</text>
      <text x="220" y="228" font-size="14" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:14px;font-weight:700;text-anchor:middle">Both sounded equally sure. Only one was right.</text>
      <rect x="20" y="242" width="400" height="76" fill="#fff" stroke="#231F20" stroke-width="1.2" style="fill:rgb(255, 255, 255);stroke:rgb(35, 31, 32);stroke-width:1.2px"></rect>
      <text x="32" y="264" font-size="13" font-weight="800" letter-spacing=".06em" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:13px;font-weight:800;letter-spacing:0.78px">WHY IT MATTERS</text>
      <text x="32" y="286" font-size="14" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:14px">Blue vs red light: with λ⁴, blue scatters about 6× more.</text>
      <text x="32" y="306" font-size="14" style="fill:rgb(35, 31, 32);font-size:14px">With the wrong λ², it would be only about 2.4×.</text>
    </g>
  </svg>

s18.chapterTitle: The answer comes home, and you check it
s18.title: Cloud AI and edge AI
s18.caption: Green marks each one's advantage. Dots stand for parameters, not to scale: big cloud models have hundreds of billions, small ones a few billion. Quantisation and distillation (chapters 4 and 8) help big models fit on devices too.

s31.title: One assistant, three pieces

s32.title: Three workflow shapes
s32.caption: In all three, people fix the steps in advance. The AI does the work inside each step.

s33.chapterTitle: Check it, vote on it, try again
s33.title: What each check has to go on
s33.caption: A check is only as good as what it checks against. Reflection has the least to go on; a vote needs some randomness (temperature) so the answers can differ.
s33.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 302" role="img" aria-labelledby="s33-ill2T s33-ill2D" width="100%">
    <title id="s33-ill2T">What each check has to go on</title>
    <desc id="s33-ill2D">Three ways a model's answer gets checked, and what each is compared with. Reflection: the model rereads its own draft with its own judgement, with nothing from outside, so it can miss its own blind spots. Evaluator: the draft is checked against a mark scheme of stated criteria, so it is only as good as its criteria. Vote: the answer is compared with other answers to the same question, such as 5p, 5p, 10p, 5p, 5p, so it only works if the answers vary.</desc>

s36.title: Who decides the steps?
s36.caption: Start on the left with the simplest design that works, and move right only when the job needs it. Safety applies whichever you choose.
s36.svg:
